summary: Specifies protecting hosts on a switched network from rogue DHCPv6 servers by filtering DHCPv6 packets at the layer 2 device. It is similar to DHCP snooping in IPv4 networks.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCPv6-Shield is a set of rules for a layer 2 switch, such as an access switch, that stop a fake DHCPv6 server from answering clients. The administrator marks the ports where the real server is connected, and the switch drops any DHCPv6 message for a client that arrives on any other port.

questions: how to block rogue dhcpv6 servers
subtitle: How a switch stops a rogue DHCPv6 server on one port from answering clients on another.

tldr.problem: Any device plugged into a switched network can answer DHCPv6 requests and hand out addresses of its own choosing, redirecting a host's traffic wherever the attacker wants.
tldr.mechanism: The switch is told which ports lead to a real DHCPv6 server or relay. On every other port it reads the whole IPv6 header chain, and if it finds a DHCPv6 message meant for a client it drops the packet and logs the event.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7610 is BCP 199 and is not obsoleted. It is the IPv6 counterpart to the DHCP snooping mechanism widely deployed in IPv4 networks, and it protects against DHCPv6 attacks only, not against router advertisements or attacks on the servers themselves.

today: RFC 7610 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 199, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. It protects against rogue DHCPv6 servers only; the document points to RFC 6105 for the equivalent protection against rogue router advertisements.

sections.title: What DHCPv6-Shield Is For
sections.content:
This document specifies DHCPv6-Shield, a mechanism for protecting hosts connected to a switched network against rogue DHCPv6 servers. The basic concept is that a layer 2 device filters DHCPv6 messages intended for DHCPv6 clients, the DHCPv6-server messages, according to a number of different criteria. The most basic filtering criterion is that DHCPv6-server messages are discarded by the layer 2 device unless they are received on specific ports of that device.

Before the device is deployed, the administrator specifies the layer 2 ports on which DHCPv6-server messages are to be allowed. Only those ports to which a DHCPv6 server or relay is to be connected should be specified. Once deployed, the device inspects received packets and passes DHCPv6-server messages only if they arrive on ports that have been explicitly configured for that purpose.

DHCPv6-Shield is analogous to the Router Advertisement Guard mechanism, intended for protection against rogue Router Advertisement messages. It mitigates only DHCPv6-based attacks against hosts: attack vectors based on other messages meant for network configuration, such as ICMPv6 Router Advertisements, are not addressed by DHCPv6-Shield itself, and it does not mitigate attacks against DHCPv6 servers such as denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer on your network that answers DHCPv6 requests can give itself any address it likes, and the traffic you send can end up somewhere else entirely. The switch is the right place to stop that, because it knows which port the real server is on. It is the same idea as DHCP snooping, which is common in IPv4 networks.

sections.title: Terms and the IPv6 Header Chain
sections.content:
DHCPv6-Shield is the set of filtering rules specified in this document, meant to mitigate attacks that employ DHCPv6-server packets. A DHCPv6-Shield device is a layer 2 device, typically a layer 2 switch, that enforces the filtering policy.

The remaining terms describe how IPv6 packets are laid out, and they matter because the rules depend on reading a packet all the way down to its DHCPv6 message. The IPv6 Header Chain contains an initial IPv6 header, zero or more IPv6 Extension Headers, and optionally a single Upper-Layer Header. If an Upper-Layer Header is present it terminates the chain; otherwise the No Next Header value, Next Header = 59, terminates it. The first member of the chain is always an IPv6 header, and a subsequent header qualifies as a member only if it is referenced by the Next Header field of the previous member. If a second IPv6 header appears in the chain, as when IPv6 is tunnelled over IPv6, it is considered an Upper-Layer Header and terminates the chain; likewise an Encapsulating Security Payload header terminates the chain.

The Upper-Layer Header is the first member of the chain that is neither an IPv6 header nor an IPv6 Extension Header, except that an ESP header or a second IPv6 header counts as one. Neither the upper-layer payload nor any protocol data following it is part of the header chain: if the Upper-Layer Header is a TCP header, the TCP payload is not part of the chain.

A First Fragment is an IPv6 fragment with a Fragment Offset equal to 0. IPv6 Extension Headers are defined in Section 4 of RFC 2460, and IANA provides a list of assigned Internet Protocol Numbers and designates which of those protocol numbers also represent IPv6 Extension Headers.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a DHCPv6 message you have to read the packet from the outside in, because IPv6 lets several optional headers sit between the IP header and the message. The chain is that sequence of headers, and it ends at the first header that is neither an IP header nor an extension header.

sections.title: Configuring the Device
sections.content:
Before being deployed for production, the DHCPv6-Shield device is explicitly configured with respect to which layer 2 ports are allowed to receive DHCPv6 packets destined to DHCPv6 clients. Only those layer 2 ports explicitly configured for that purpose are allowed to receive such packets and pass them to the clients.

The configuration is therefore a list of ports. The administrator decides which ports lead to a real DHCPv6 server or to a relay that forwards to one, and every other port is a port from which DHCPv6-server messages must not be accepted. The device applies the filtering rules of Section 5 on the ports that are not in the allowed list.
sections.plainLanguage: Configuration is one decision: which ports are allowed to send DHCPv6 replies to clients. Everything else follows from that list, and the device applies its rules to every port that is not on it.

sections.title: The Filtering Rules
sections.content:
The following filtering rules are enforced on those ports that are not allowed to receive DHCPv6 packets destined to DHCPv6 clients.

  • Parse the whole header chain. Implementations must parse the entire IPv6 Header Chain present in the packet to identify whether or not it is a DHCPv6 packet meant for a DHCPv6 client. They must not enforce a limit on the number of bytes they can inspect, since that could introduce false negatives: a DHCPv6-server packet received on a port not allowed to receive such packets could be allowed simply because the device does not parse the entire header chain.
  • Drop a first fragment that is incomplete. If the packet is a First Fragment and it fails to contain the entire IPv6 Header Chain, the device must drop the packet and ought to log the drop event as a security fault. Such packets could otherwise be used to circumvent DHCPv6-Shield, since RFC 7112 requires that the First Fragment contain the entire header chain. This rule applies only to fragments with a Fragment Offset of 0; non-first fragments can safely be passed, since they will never reassemble into a complete datagram if they are part of a DHCPv6 packet meant for a client received on a port where such packets are not allowed.
  • Drop unknown next headers. The device must provide a configuration knob that controls whether packets with unrecognized Next Header values are dropped, and that knob must default to drop. An unrecognized Next Header value could identify an extension header and thus be used to conceal a DHCPv6-server packet, since there is no way to parse past an unrecognized value.
  • Drop the identified server message. If the packet is identified as a DHCPv6 packet meant for a DHCPv6 client, the device must drop it and should log the drop event as a security alert.
  • Pass everything else. In all other cases the device must pass the packet as usual. For the purpose of enforcing the filtering policy, an ESP header should be considered an upper-layer protocol, so packets employing ESP are passed to the intended destination.

If a packet is dropped by the policy, the drop should be logged in an implementation-specific manner as a security fault, and it is useful for the logging mechanism to include a per-port drop counter dedicated to DHCPv6-Shield packet drops.

Rule 2 exists so that packets which cannot be positively identified as not being DHCPv6-server packets are dropped by default, which means DHCPv6-Shield could in theory block some legitimate packets. Since IPv6 packets that fail to include the entire header chain are virtually impossible to police with stateless filters and firewalls, they are unlikely to survive in real networks, and RFC 7112 requires that hosts employing fragmentation include the entire header chain in the First Fragment, which eliminates those false positives. The rules also implicitly handle fragmented packets: if the device fails to identify the upper-layer protocol as a result of fragmentation, the corresponding packets are dropped.

Finally, IPv6 implementations that allow overlapping fragments, that is, that do not comply with RFC 5722, might still be subject to DHCPv6-based attacks, although an assessment of IPv6 implementations seems to indicate that most current implementations comply with RFC 5722.
sections.plainLanguage: On a port that is not allowed to send DHCPv6, the switch reads the packet from the top down. If it cannot read far enough to be sure what the packet is, it drops it. If it finds a DHCPv6 message addressed to a client, it drops it and records it. Anything else is passed on unchanged. The strict reading is deliberate: a rule that stopped after a fixed number of bytes would let an attacker hide a message just beyond that point.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The recommendations in the document represent the ideal behaviour of a DHCPv6-Shield device. To implement it on the fast path, it may be necessary to limit the depth into the packet that can be scanned before giving up. Where there is such a limitation, implementations are recommended to drop packets after attempting to find a protocol header up to that limit. Ideally such devices should be configurable with a list of protocol header identifiers, so that new transport protocols standardized after the device was released can be added to the list of header types it recognizes. Since any protocol header that is not a UDP header would be passed by the DHCPv6-Shield algorithm, this lets such devices avoid blocking the use of new transport protocols. When an implementation must stop searching for recognizable header types because of such a limitation, the device should be configurable to either pass or drop that packet.

The mechanism can be used to mitigate DHCPv6-based attacks against hosts. Attack vectors based on other messages meant for network configuration, such as ICMPv6 Router Advertisements, are out of scope, and the mechanism does not mitigate attacks against DHCPv6 servers such as denial of service.

If deployed in a layer 2 domain with several cascading switches, there will be an ingress port on the host's local switch that will need to be enabled for receiving DHCPv6-server messages. That local switch will be reliant on the upstream devices filtering out rogue messages, as it has no way of determining which upstream DHCP-server messages are valid. In order to be effective, DHCPv6-Shield should therefore be deployed and enabled on all layer 2 switches of a given layer 2 domain.

If an attacker sends a fragmented DHCPv6 packet on a port not allowed to receive such packets, the First Fragment is dropped and the rest of the fragments are passed. The victim node would then tie memory buffers for those fragments, which would never reassemble into a complete datagram. If a large number of such packets were sent and the victim node failed to implement proper resource management for the fragment reassembly buffer, this could lead to a denial of service, but it does not really introduce a new attack vector, since an attacker could always perform the same attack with a forged fragmented datagram in which at least one fragment is missing.

The security of a site employing DHCPv6-Shield could be further improved by deploying RFC 7513 to mitigate IPv6 address spoofing attacks. Other mechanisms for mitigating attacks based on DHCPv6-server messages are available with different deployment considerations; for example, the Secure DHCPv6 work allows authentication of DHCPv6-server packets if the IPv6 addresses of the DHCPv6 servers can be pre-configured at the client nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two practical points. The switch has to be set up on every switch in the building, not just one, because a downstream switch cannot tell whether a message from upstream is genuine. And on fast hardware you may have to limit how deep the switch reads; in that case it must drop what it cannot classify, or configure what it does with it.

viz.caption: THE FIVE FILTERING RULES FOR A PORT THAT MAY NOT SEND DHCPv6

items.title: 1. Read the whole header chain
items.text: No limit on how many bytes may be inspected, so a server message cannot hide beyond a fixed depth.

items.title: 2. Drop incomplete first fragments
items.text: A first fragment that does not contain the whole header chain is dropped and logged as a security fault.

items.title: 3. Drop unknown next headers
items.text: A configuration knob controls this, and it defaults to drop.

items.title: 4. Drop the identified server message
items.text: A DHCPv6 packet meant for a client is dropped and logged as a security alert.

items.title: 5. Pass everything else
items.text: In all other cases the packet is passed as usual.

viz.caption: THE SAME PACKET, ON AN ALLOWED PORT AND ON A FORBIDDEN ONE

left.title: Allowed port
left.desc: The port is configured for DHCPv6, so the message is passed to the client.

right.title: Port not allowed
right.desc: The message is a DHCPv6-server message on a forbidden port, so it is dropped and logged.

children.label: Upper-Layer Header
children.note: Optional; an ESP header or a second IPv6 header ends the chain here
